analysis.one_liner: Overhauls Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and the tax code with private accounts, benefit cuts, and major tax reductions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2010 with 15 Republican cosponsors, the bill went to six House committees and subcommittees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restructure the country's major retirement and health programs. It would turn Medicaid into fixed grants to states, repeal the children's health program (CHIP), create a new Medicare program for future retirees with a higher eligibility age, and let workers put part of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts. It would also eliminate the estate tax, the taxes on capital gains, dividends, and interest, the individual alternative minimum tax, and the corporate income tax (replaced with a tax on business sales), while giving every uninsured person a tax credit to buy private insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people would get a refundable tax credit (about $2,300 per adult and $1,700 per child) paid directly toward private insurance premiums. High-income households gain the most financially: the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and taxes on capital gains, dividends, and interest would all disappear. Corporations would see their income tax repealed and replaced with a tax on sales. Health insurers would gain because the credits and exchanges route coverage through private plans, and financial firms would gain from managing new personal Social Security accounts.

how_it_helps.text: Creates state-based exchanges where private health plans compete for enrollees, with guaranteed access and limits on pre-existing condition exclusions for people buying on the exchange [S2][S3].

Provides a refundable, advanceable tax credit for private health insurance — $2,300 per adult and $1,700 per child, capped at $5,700 per family — paid directly to insurers on behalf of enrollees [S2][S3].

Allows health insurers to sell individual plans in every state under the rules of whichever single state the insurer designates as its 'primary state,' so plans avoid other states' coverage mandates and rate rules [S3].

Repeals the alternative minimum tax, lets taxpayers elect a simplified two-rate system, and excludes all capital gains, dividends, and interest from taxable income; it also repeals the estate and gift taxes [S2].
Repeals the corporate income tax and replaces it with a border-adjustable business consumption tax, which its authors argue would make U.S. businesses more competitive [S2][S3].

Lets workers direct part of their Social Security contributions into personal savings accounts they could pass on to heirs, and sets new discretionary and total federal spending limits through 2083 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Seniors and future retirees would bear the largest changes: Medicare would become a new program for people becoming eligible in 2021 with a raised eligibility age and income-based reductions in the drug premium subsidy, and Social Security's normal retirement age would phase up to 67. Low-income families would see Medicaid converted to fixed state grants and the CHIP children's program repealed. Workers who use the tax credit would lose the tax-free treatment of employer health coverage, and consumers would pay the new business consumption tax passed through in prices.

drawbacks.text: Medicaid becomes a program of fixed grants to states designed to slow spending growth, and the State Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) is repealed outright [S2].

Establishes a separate Medicare program for new beneficiaries beginning in 2021, raises the Medicare eligibility age, and reduces the Part D drug premium subsidy based on income — meaning a less generous benefit for future retirees [S2].
Replaces part of Social Security with personal savings accounts subject to market risk and phases the normal retirement age up to 67 by 2021 [S2].
Workers who claim the health credit lose the exclusion for employer-provided health coverage, so the health benefits most working families get through their jobs would become taxable income [S3].

The largest tax changes — repealing the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and all taxes on capital gains, dividends, and interest — apply to forms of income held overwhelmingly by the wealthiest households, while the replacement business consumption tax is paid on sales of goods and services [S2].

Medical liability provisions would force speedier resolution of malpractice claims and channel disputes toward alternatives to jury trials, and grant programs would push states toward 'health court' alternatives to tort litigation [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real help to the uninsured through its tax credit and would put long-term federal spending on a stricter legal footing. But those gains come bundled with the largest redistribution in the bill: the tax changes concentrate their benefit on the wealthiest households and on corporations, while the cost is borne by future retirees (a later, higher Medicare eligibility age and private-portfolio retirement risk), low-income families (Medicaid block grants and the repeal of CHIP), and working families whose employer health coverage becomes taxable. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the plan trades broad, well-understood public programs for tax cuts and individually held accounts.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in January 2010, the bill was referred to six House committees and then to subcommittees on health, Social Security, and education, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Paul Ryan (R-WI) introduced the bill on January 27, 2010, with 7 original co-sponsors named on the bill and 15 cosponsors total, all Republicans [S1][S3][S4].

It was referred to Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Rules, Budget, and Judiciary, and then to subcommittees on Health, Social Security, Higher Education, and Health Employment Labor and Pensions between late January and February 2010 [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, current Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and Social Security benefits continued unchanged and the estate, capital gains, and corporate tax cuts never took effect. Seniors, people with disabilities, and low-income families kept the existing programs; high-income households and corporations did not get the tax changes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors and Medicaid families kept existing benefits

for.name: Paul Ryan
for.role: U.S. Representative (WI-1), House Budget Committee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Roadmap for America's Future Act of 2010, a comprehensive rewrite of health care, Social Security, taxes, and the budget process.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Her majority never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it remained parked in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 named sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled House (253 Democrats to 178 Republicans) never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill routes coverage help through private insurers: tax credits are paid to insurance companies, exchanges exist to let private plans compete, and CHIP is repealed in favor of private options. It also lets insurers sell plans across state lines under one state's lighter rules, weakening state coverage mandates — help for affordability comes bundled with deregulation.

Repealing the estate tax, the AMT, and all taxes on capital gains, dividends, and interest eliminates nearly every tax on wealth and investment income. Meanwhile the replacement business consumption tax falls on the sale of goods and services everyone buys.
The corporate income tax is repealed and replaced with a tax on business sales, shifting the burden from corporate profits toward consumption prices.

Personal Social Security savings accounts would steer payroll contributions into private investments managed by the fund industry, while workers — not the industry — bear the market risk to their guaranteed benefit.

Medical liability reform would require speedy resolution of malpractice claims and fund state alternatives to tort litigation, reducing providers' legal exposure and patients' recourse for negligent care.
The bill reduces Medicare hospital payment updates ('market basket increases'), slowing the growth of hospital revenue.
